sec1.lens: This is the architectural x-ray — if the presenter can't sketch the entire webinar on a napkin before they touch a single slide, they've already lost the room.
emphasis: Force them to recite the full arc (Origin Story -> Big Domino -> Three Secrets -> Stack -> Close) from memory before any design work — architecture lives in the head, not the deck
Prework gates matter: no headline, no 3 secrets, no offer stack = no slide build. Period.
The 'foundation of the house' metaphor is correct but too soft. This is load-bearing. Skip one piece and the close collapses and you blame the close.
common_traps: Novices skim the framework overview and jump to making pretty slides — they confuse aesthetics with architecture
Treating the prework as optional 'reminder' rather than a hard gate
Not being able to explain why each block exists — they memorize the map but don't understand what job each block does in the buyer's brain
voice_notes: If you can't draw this on a cocktail napkin, you don't own it yet.
Every block on this map is earning its seat. If you can't tell me what JOB a block is doing in the buyer's brain, cut it or learn it.
Foundation of the house? Yeah. And the house is on fire if you skip a brick.

sec2.lens: The opening eight slides are the single highest-leverage real estate in the entire presentation — this is where you earn the right to be listened to, and most presenters blow it by being cute instead of commanding.
emphasis: Bold Promise must be SPECIFIC enough that the listener can picture the outcome in five seconds — vague promises = vague attention
Take Control is not optional — if they keep Slack open, you already lost the sale. The hourly-rate framing ('you'd pay me $500/hr for this') is the play.
Street Cred beats Qualify Yourself — other people's results land 10x harder than your own. Front-load the student wins.
Hook-To-The-End is a commitment device — without it, 40% of your audience is gone by the teaching block. Make the bonus concrete, not vague.
One Sentence Persuasion (Blair Warren) is the secret weapon — weave it into the intro, not just add it as a slide. All five elements, one sentence, delivered with weight.
common_traps: Boasting on Qualify Yourself instead of lifting others up — instant credibility destruction
Future Pacing written as generic 'imagine your dream life' fluff instead of a specific scenario tied to their actual pain
Take Control being apologetic ('sorry to ask, but...') instead of commanding — you are paying them in value, act like it
Skipping Hook-To-The-End because 'my content is good enough to keep them' — that's arrogance, not data
Bold Promise that is a feature promise instead of a transformation promise ('I'll teach you X' vs 'by the end you'll know how to Y')
voice_notes: Specificity is credibility. 'Make more money' is noise. 'Add $10K to your business in 30 days without hiring' is signal.
Your credibility slide is where the sale is either made possible or killed. Lift others, don't beat your chest.
If Slack dings and they pick up their phone, you just lost the sale. Take Control or take the loss.
Blair's One Sentence is the most underused weapon in this whole deck. Write it, memorize it, deliver it like a closing argument.

sec3.lens: Breakouts aren't feedback sessions — they're pattern-recognition drills. You learn more from watching five other decks than from anyone commenting on yours.
emphasis: Speed over polish — fast share forces structural clarity
Eyes over ears — observe what's working in others' decks, study, adapt, honor the structure
Don't hunt for validation, hunt for gaps
common_traps: Turning breakout into a mini-pitch to feel good
Spending 15 minutes on one deck and nobody else shares
Writing down feedback instead of watching what lands when others share
voice_notes: Breakouts aren't therapy. Share fast, watch harder.
The best intel in the room is what other people are getting wrong AND right. Stay present.
If you leave the breakout without one structural idea to adapt, you slept through it.

sec4.lens: This is the engine of the entire webinar — Epiphany Bridge is the single most important story-technology in persuasion and 80% of presenters fake their way through it.
emphasis: False Beliefs must be SPECIFIC to this audience — generic beliefs ('I'm not good enough') don't move money. 'Funnels are too technical for non-techies' moves money.
The Wall must be real and painful — if the wall is fake, the epiphany is fake, and the whole bridge collapses under its own weight
Emotion FIRST, then logic — the ah-ha is the permission slip that lets them accept the techno babble. Reverse it and you get a skeptic.
All 8 elements are non-negotiable — skip the Conflict and the story feels too easy; skip the Transformation and the story has no payoff
The story is NOT about you — it's a Trojan horse carrying a new belief into their head. Always serve the belief.
common_traps: Writing the epiphany bridge as a resume or origin story — 'here's what I did' — instead of an emotional journey
Making the Desires too shallow (only external, no internal) — you need both the 'I want money' AND the 'I want to prove my father wrong'
Skipping the Conflict because it feels uncomfortable to share — but conflict is where trust is earned
Identifying false beliefs based on what YOU think they believe instead of what they actually tell themselves at 2am
Making the epiphany feel convenient/lucky instead of earned — 'then I met a guy who told me' lands hollow
voice_notes: The epiphany bridge is the most powerful persuasion structure on planet earth. Learn it, drill it, live it.
If your Wall isn't making YOU uncomfortable to tell, it's not big enough. Real stakes, real story.
You're not telling them your story. You're carrying a new belief into their brain wrapped in your story.
Emotion is the password. Logic is what you do AFTER you're inside. Get that order wrong and you're locked out.

sec5.lens: Framework-first share is a structural stress test — if the skeleton doesn't hold up when you say it out loud in 60 seconds, the full story is a house of cards.
emphasis: Skeleton first, meat later — if you can't summarize in one pass, the arc is broken
Feedback on structure not style — style is personal, structure is mechanical
Notice what questions people ask when you share — those are the gaps in your arc
common_traps: Telling the full story instead of the framework — eats everyone's time
Getting defensive about feedback on the outline — the outline isn't sacred, the sale is
Skipping this step because 'I'll tell it better with the slides' — no you won't, you'll just hide the weakness
voice_notes: If the skeleton can't walk, the body's dead. Frame first.
60 seconds to share the bones. If it takes longer, your arc is broken.
The questions people ask after you share? Those ARE the gaps. Fix them.

sec6.lens: Slides are prompts for you, the presenter — not billboards for the audience. If they're reading your slides, they're not listening to your story, and story is what sells.
emphasis: Raw-over-polished is mission critical — stock photos scream 'salesman,' Facebook photos scream 'I'm like you'
Each slide = one emotional beat, not one teaching point — this is a story, not a class
15-minute timer on the origin block is SACRED — run long and you bleed into teaching time and the whole thing falls apart
Image choice tells the audience whether to trust you — pick images that carry the emotion, not the info
common_traps: Walls of text because 'I want to make sure I don't forget' — use speaker notes for that, not slides
Polished stock photos because 'I want to look professional' — you want to look REAL. Professional = suspect.
Running 25 minutes on origin because the story is juicy — you just robbed your teaching block
One slide per sentence — kills the pace. One slide per beat.
voice_notes: Slides are a teleprompter for you. They're not a textbook for them.
Raw photos beat stock photos 10 out of 10 times. Real beats polished.
The 15-minute timer is not a suggestion. It's the difference between a tight webinar and a bloated mess.
One beat, one slide. If the slide has five bullet points, it's five slides.

sec7.lens: Emotion check BEFORE logic build — if the origin slides don't make the room lean in, no amount of framework polish downstream will save the close.
emphasis: Are they leaning in? If not, your emotional beats are off — fix them here before you build Secret #1
Missing visual cues = missing emotion — find them now
Watch for the silence — the places where nobody reacts are the places you're losing them
common_traps: Getting style feedback ('change the font') instead of emotion feedback ('I didn't feel the Wall')
Moving forward to framework build when the origin still isn't landing — you're building on sand
Not being honest about whether you felt something when others shared — be the honest mirror they need
voice_notes: If nobody leans in, nobody buys. Fix emotion here or die later.
The silence in a breakout is the signal. Where nobody reacts, they're not connecting.
Don't let them move forward until the origin actually lands. You're doing them a favor.

sec8.lens: Strategy vs. Tactics is THE line that separates webinars that sell from webinars that teach their way out of a sale — this is the single most violated rule in this whole framework.
emphasis: Strategy (WHAT) in the webinar, Tactics (HOW) in the product — cross that line and you've given the milk away
Story-Strategy-Social Proof is the rhythm — hit that cadence every single Secret
Social proof isn't a testimonial slide at the end — it's woven into the teaching so every strategy point is validated in real-time
The story of how you LEARNED or EARNED the framework is as important as the framework itself — it's the credibility anchor
30-minute block = 3 frameworks at 10 min each OR one deeper framework — but whichever you choose, hit the formula cleanly
common_traps: Teaching the step-by-step because 'if I over-deliver they'll trust me' — wrong. If you over-deliver they feel satisfied and DON'T BUY.
Skipping the 'how I learned' story and jumping straight into the framework — now it's theory, not experience
Treating social proof as a single slide instead of a drumbeat throughout
Teaching a framework that isn't actually connected to the Big Domino — feels like content-filler
Getting so excited about the teaching that you blow past the 30-minute budget and lose the close
voice_notes: The moment you teach HOW, you just sold them the ability to NOT buy.
WHAT in the webinar, HOW in the product. Period. End of discussion.
Story, Strategy, Social Proof. That's the heartbeat. Skip a beat and they walk.
Over-delivering on free content is the amateur's move. Professionals deliver VALUE, not COMPLETION.
Social proof isn't a slide at the end. It's oxygen — you need it every few minutes or the room suffocates.

sec9.lens: Breakout here is about pressure-testing the strategy-vs-tactics line — did they hold it, or did they leak the how?
emphasis: Listen for leaks — every time a peer gives away a tactic, flag it. That leak will cost them sales.
Bullet points are enough — this is about arc, not polish
Is the framework connected to the Big Domino? If not, it's orphan content.
common_traps: Giving away tactics in the breakout 'just to show it works' — you're training the wrong muscle
Polishing slides instead of testing structure — wasted breakout
Failing to flag when a peer is crossing the strategy-tactics line — you're not doing them any favors by being polite
voice_notes: Listen for the leak. Every tactic given away in practice becomes a tactic given away in the live.
Bullets beat beauty at this stage. Prove the arc works naked.
If the framework isn't serving the Big Domino, cut it. Orphan content kills pace.

sec10.lens: Prework is where next week's success is born or killed — the presenters who show up with Secrets #2 and #3 already drafted will outperform the ones who wing it by 3x, guaranteed.
emphasis: Secret #2 = Internal belief (the story they tell themselves about themselves) — hardest to shift, highest leverage
Secret #3 = External belief (the story they tell themselves about the world) — shifts the ecosystem narrative
Three legs per framework: Story, Strategy, Tactics-prep — don't show up with just an outline, show up with the story ALREADY TOLD once out loud
Community brainstorm is a force multiplier — the presenters who workshop with peers before the session outperform
If they don't have Secret #2 and #3 drafted, they don't have a webinar — they have a half-baked intro with a cliff
common_traps: Showing up to next session with only Secret #1 polished — now they're scrambling and the back half will be weak
Drafting frameworks without checking connection to the Big Domino — orphan frameworks waste time
Skipping the community check — ego says 'I got this,' reality says 'an outside eye finds the holes'
Treating prework as optional homework instead of the actual deliverable
voice_notes: Next week is won this week. Prework isn't homework — it's the real work.
Internal belief is the hardest shift and the most profitable one. Don't half-ass Secret #2.
Show up with all three legs already standing, or you'll limp through the whole session.
If your framework doesn't serve the Big Domino, it's content, not persuasion. Cut it.
